desc:
The array hours records how many hours an employee worked on each consecutive day. A day is tiring if the employee worked strictly more than 8 hours, otherwise it is a normal day.

A stretch of consecutive days is well-performing if it contains strictly more tiring days than normal days. Return the length of the longest well-performing stretch (0 if there is none).

hours = [9, 9, 6, 0, 6, 6, 9]
longest stretch: [9, 9, 6] (two tiring days, one normal)
result = 3
hints: Convert each day to +1 (tiring) or -1 (normal). A stretch is well-performing exactly when its sum is positive.
With prefix sums s, you want the longest range with s[j] - s[i] > 0. If the whole prefix s[j] is already positive, the stretch can start at day 1.

Otherwise s[j] is zero or negative. Because the prefix moves by only +1 or -1, the earliest earlier prefix that is smaller than s[j] must have the value exactly s[j] - 1. Store the first index of each prefix value in a dictionary.
editorial: Map days to +1/-1 and take prefix sums s. We need the maximum j - i with s[j] > s[i]. If s[j] > 0 then i = 0 works and the stretch is the whole prefix. If s[j] ≤ 0, we need some earlier prefix with a smaller value. Prefix sums change by one unit at a time, so the walk starts at 0, which is at least s[j], so to reach any smaller value it must first step onto s[j] - 1. Hence the first time the walk hits the value s[j] - 1 is the earliest index holding a smaller value.
So record the first index at which each value is seen and, for every j, look up s[j] - 1. One pass, O(n) time and O(n) space. A monotonic stack over prefix sums also solves it but is more code.
